content:
Most founders edit for length. That's the wrong target.
---
Paul Graham reread his own essay and flagged something rare: long at the macro, tight at the micro. No bloat. That distinction is the whole game.
---
Length ≠ bloat. Brevity ≠ clarity.

Your pitch deck can be 20 slides and razor sharp. Your memo can be 2 pages and completely hollow. The variable is fat — not length.
---
The editing question isn't "how do I make this shorter?"

It's "does every sentence earn its place?"

Cut the fat. Keep the substance. Those are different operations.
---
Founders who communicate with density win the room, close the round, align the team faster.

Writing is leverage. Most people treat it like a chore.
---
Do you edit for length or for density? Be honest.
source_story_title: Paul Graham Reflects on 'How to Do Great Work' — Dense but Lean Writing
source_story_summary: Paul Graham reread his essay 'How to Do Great Work' and noted an unusual quality: it is long at the macro level but unusually tight at the micro level, with little fat. This combination — length without bloat — is rare and noteworthy, and he shared the essay link alongside his observation.

content:
YC just stress-tested a startup plan against the "OpenAI takes everything" scenario. It survived. That's not a win — that's the new minimum bar.

---

The real signal: model-layer commoditization is no longer a thought experiment. It's a live planning constraint at the best accelerator in the world. Your moat question has changed.

---

Old moat question: "Can we defensibly outcompete rivals in our category?"

New moat question: "Does our business survive if our API provider becomes our direct competitor tomorrow?"

If you can't answer that clearly, you don't have a strategy. You have a dependency.

---

The founders who win this cycle will build at the intersection of two things AI can't easily replicate: proprietary data loops and human-trust surfaces. Everything else is rented ground.

---

Most AI startups today are building on someone else's platform AND in someone else's market. That's not a company. That's a feature waiting to be acqui-killed.

---

The move: design your business so the model layer becoming a commodity makes you stronger, not extinct. Switching costs, data network effects, workflow lock-in. Stack them.

---

What's your honest answer to the new moat question? Does your plan survive if your foundation model provider goes vertical into your market? Drop it below — I'll tell you what I see.
source_story_title: YC Office Hours Produce AI-Resilient Business Strategy — A Notable First
source_story_summary: During a YC office hours session, Paul Graham and a startup developed a business plan designed to remain viable even in a scenario where AI model companies (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) have captured all adjacent markets. Graham called this outcome 'a first,' signaling that the existential threat of model-layer commoditization is now a live strategic variable in YC conversations.
